## 1. Irregular verbs

In Latin as in all natural languages, irregular verbs are numerous, and are among the most commonly used words (if they were little used, they would not have enough vitality to keep their irregular form and would be, in one way or another, replaced by regular verbs). It is therefore important to know them, and for that, nothing replaces USAGE.

However, we are going to propose to you a way of knowing them better without waiting until you have practised them a great deal. From now on, we will point out these verbs<sup>1</sup> to you with an asterisk: for example: fert\*. Each time you meet this indication, refer to the grammatical appendix (p. 510 to 517). When you have found the verb indicated there, note its peculiarities on a sheet that you will keep from now on in your book. Then, when you meet it again, make sure that you know its conjugation well. Each time you are in doubt, look at your notes again and, if they are deficient, complete them by referring once more to the grammatical appendix.

Example: you meet the verb ferre, *to carry*, or one of its compounds (afferre, *to bring*; proferre, *to push, to utter*, etc.). On your sheet, already note its principal tenses: fero, fers, ferre, tuli, latum.<sup>2</sup> Then, each time you find this verb again in any form, first check that you know its five principal tenses well, then gradually complete the section by noting its other irregularities.<sup>3</sup>

If you are content to know its principal tenses alone, you could already conjugate the verb in question in a way that is almost understandable, and with a rigour acceptable for conversation. But if you want to write a letter or if you wish, as we hope, to speak correctly, you will have to look more closely at the grammatical appendix and note all the irregularities that slip into certain tenses.

Thus for ferre, you will discover:

- the PRESENT ACTIVE INDICATIVE which, for the reason we indicated above, is the tense that has the most irregularities: fero, **fers**, **fert**, ferimus, **fertis**, ferunt; the irregularity is the absence of the i in the 2nd and 3rd pers. sg. and the 2nd pl., marked in bold;
- the PRESENT PASSIVE INDICATIVE: feror, ferris (two r, for it is the contraction of fereris), fertur, ferimur, ferimini, feruntur;
- the IMPERFECT SUBJUNCTIVE where an e is missing in all persons in the active: ferrem, ferres, etc., and in the passive: ferrer, ferreris, ferretur, etc. (instead of fererem, etc.);
- the same absence of an e in the ACTIVE INFINITIVE: ferre (for ferere) and PASSIVE ferri; as well as in the PRESENT ACTIVE IMPERATIVE: fer, *carry*, ferte, *carry* (pl.) (for ferite); PASSIVE ferre, ferimini;
- the FUTURE IMPERATIVE (existing only in the active): ferto, fertote. The other tenses of the INFECTUM (series of the present) are regular (imperfect, ferebam; future, feram, feres, etc.);
- the PERFECTUM (series of the perfect) where another verb is used: tuli, tulisti, etc., for the perfect indicative, tulerim, etc., for the perfect subjunctive; tuleram (subj. tulissem) for the pluperfect and tulero for the future perfect; without any other irregularity than the use of this new radical;
- finally that the same goes for the SUPINE latum and the PERFECT PASSIVE PARTICIPLE: latus (-a, -um) sum, es, etc., *I have been carried*; as well as for the other tenses of the PASSIVE PERFECTUM.

You see that in the end this verb is not as nasty as it might have seemed: if you remember the principal tenses and the fact that, sometimes, an e evaporates, a little flair is enough for you to get out of it without great risk of errors. But check from time to time that your flair is not deceiving you!

## 2. The principal tenses

For most Latin verbs, only the formation of the principal tenses poses a few problems. Once these tenses are known, their conjugation is obtained entirely regularly.

Moreover, this formation of the principal tenses, if it does not follow absolute rules, nevertheless follows certain laws whose existence you may have suspected.

Let us therefore see how our four conjugations behave:

### A. 1st and 4th conjugations

You may have noticed that their PERFECT was often in -vi (with an alternative form in -ii for the 4th) and their supine even more often in -tum. Examples:

- 1st conjugation: amo, -as, -are, avi, atum, *to love*;
- 4th conjugation: audio, -is, -ire, ivi (or ii), itum, *to hear*.

However, there are exceptions, for example, 1st conjugation: do, das, dare, dedi, datum, *to give*; cubo, -as, -are, cubui, cubitum, *to lie down*; 4th conjugation: venio, -is, -ire, veni, ventum, *to come*.

### B. 2nd conjugation

Likewise, for the second conjugation, the PERFECT is often in -ui and the SUPINE in -itum: debeo, -es, -ere, ui, itum; likewise teneo, *to hold*; placeo, *to please*, etc.

But we also have:

- moveo, -es, -ere, movi, motum, *to move*;
- rideo, -es, -ere, risi, risum, *to laugh*;
- mordeo, -es, -ere, momordi, morsum, *to bite*.

### C. 3rd conjugation

But it is in the 3rd conjugation and the mixed 3rd that the variety is most remarkable. Here are a few examples of the most common formations (classified according to that of the perfect):

| | Formation of the perfect | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| a) | Stem of the perfect identical to that of the present | volvo, -is, -ere, volvi, volutum, *to roll*; or differing only in quantity and accentuation: ĕdit, *he eats*, but ēdit, *he ate*; and likewise in the 4th conj.: evĕnit, present (cf. L. 62, N. 14), but evēnit, perfect |
| b) | Doubling of a syllable | cano, -is, -ere, cecini, cantum, *to sing*; cado, -is, -ere, cecidi, casum, *to fall* |
| c) | Change of vowel | ago, -is, -ere, egi, actum, *to push* |
| d) | Change of consonant | nubo, -is, -ere, nupsi, nuptum, *to marry*; dico, -is, -ere, dixi, dictum, *to say*; uro, -is, -ere, ussi, ustum, *to burn* |
| e) | Perfects in -vi or -ui (which was formerly written in the same way) | cupio, -is, -ere, cupivi (or cupii), cupitum, *to desire* (mixed 3rd); colo, -is, -ere, colui, cultum, *to cultivate* |
| f) | Shortening | obstupesco, -is, -ere, obstupui, no supine, *to be stupefied* |

So much for the formation of the perfect!

That of the supine is easier to retain: indeed it is the one that provides the most numerous derivatives, and in particular those whose trace is easily found in English and French. Thus, following the order of the verbs given above, we find: amateur, auditor, date, cubitus, (ad)venture, debtor, (e)motion, risible, morsel, volute, cantatrice, case, act, nuptial, dictum, (comb)ustion, cult.

You can see from this list that all the supines except one (cupitum) have given a derivative, to what extent Latin has rubbed off on our languages: even if you did not manage to draw from our method all the profit we hope, you could at least be sure that you will not have wasted your time learning to know better the language to which yours owes the best of itself.

SECOND WAVE: the 14th lesson.

---

1. With the exception of the verb esse, whose conjugation you must now know through usage.
2. Which you will find in table 41 of the grammatical appendix.
3. Which you will find in the paragraph to which table 41 refers you; e.g. § 37 in the case of fero.
